articles.title: New Mac Studio M5 Max and M5 Ultra: Everything you need to know
articles.subtitle: Macworld New Mac Studio 2026: At a glance What’s new: The 2026 Mac Studio gains M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, dramatically faster AI and graphics performance, faster SSD storage, increased memory bandwidth, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and enhanced professional...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
New Mac Studio 2026: At a glance

What’s new: The 2026 Mac Studio gains M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, dramatically faster AI and graphics performance, faster SSD storage, increased memory bandwidth, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and enhanced professional connectivity.

Release date: Announced on August 25, 2026

Price: From $2,499/£2,499

Pre-orders: Pre-order now

On sale: Shipping starts on September 22, 2026 but the Mac Studio with 512GB of unified memory is coming in late October.

Apple has launched a new Mac Studio to replace the M4 Max and M3 Ultra model introduced 17 months ago, in March 2025. Externally, the 2026 Mac Studio retains what Apple calls its “signature compact design,” with the most significant upgrades taking place inside.

The previous generation was unusual because it mixed chip generations, pairing M4 Max with M3 Ultra. The 2026 models bring both tiers into the M5 family, with M5 Max and the new M5 Ultra. M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU and up to a 40-core GPU, while M5 Ultra scales to a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU. Neural Accelerators are now built into every GPU core to boost AI performance.

Apple claims up to 1. 3x faster CPU performance, 1. 8x faster graphics and 4. 3x faster AI performance, depending on the configuration and workload. M5 Max also adds third-generation hardware-accelerated ray tracing, while M5 Ultra can play up to 33 streams of 8K ProRes 422 video simultaneously.

Elsewhere, PCIe Gen 6-based SSDs deliver up to twice the storage performance, while Apple’s N1 chip adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. USB-C genlock, support for up to eight displays, and Thunderbolt 5 clustering for distributed AI workloads are also new.

When is the new Mac Studio available?

The new Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra was announced on August 25, 2026, but it won’t start shipping until September 22. Even then, not every configuration will be available: Apple says Mac Studio models configured with 512GB of unified memory won’t arrive until “late October.”

You can pre-order the new Mac Studio now, though, and if you want one we’d recommend ordering early. Ongoing chip and component shortages have constrained Mac availability, so the most popular configurations could quickly become difficult to find.

Pre-order the Mac Studio at Apple U.K.

How much does the new Mac Studio cost?

Has the Mac Studio price gone up?

In June 2026, Apple raised the starting price of the Mac Studio by $500, from $1,999 to $2,499. The M3 Ultra model saw an even steeper increase, rising $1,300 from its $3,999 launch price to $5,299. The hikes were part of broader increases across the Mac lineup, which Apple attributed to sharply higher component costs, particularly RAM.

articles.title: The Potential of M6 and M5 Ultra for Local AI on macOS
articles.subtitle: Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio. You can read more details about the announcement and related specs in John’s overview.

As someone who’s been working with an M3 Ultra Mac Studio (on loan from Apple) with 512 GB of RAM for the past year (plus two separate M4 Mac minis) with a particular focus on local AI models and performance gains enabled by Apple’s MLX framework, I obviously am very interested in these new machines.

To give you some context: my current workspace for my upcoming iOS and iPadOS 27 review, which lives in Notion, is entirely managed by a series of local agents running the latest DeepSeek-V4-Flash via MLX on the Mac Studio, which continuously scan the project for new notes, sources, and research material that is automatically categorized and linked in the chapters that I’m writing.

So, yes, I’m sure I’ll have more thoughts on the new Mac minis and Mac Studios soon. In the meantime, I thought it’d be fun to break down the local AI-related details from Apple.

First, the M6. While it may not be the powerhouse that the M5 Ultra is, it’s an interesting new chip because of its new 2 nm process and dual Neural Engine system:

M6 is built using cutting-edge 2 nm process technology, packing greater transistor density into a smaller die for a major leap in performance and power efficiency. M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

But that’s not all: the new 12-core GPU (which has two more cores than the M4’s old GPU) now features Neural Accelerators in each core for the first time on the Mac mini. The result, according to Apple, is “4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than Mac mini with M4”. If these numbers hold up and scale linearly, a local Mixture-of-Experts model such as Qwen 3.

5-35B-A3B, which would run at ~17 tokens/sec on average on a base M4 Mac mini with 16 GB of RAM, could realistically generate output at over 60 tokens/second with the base model M6 Mac mini.

Based on what we’ve seen so far, the one downside of the M6 Mac mini is that it does not have Thunderbolt 5 ports; those are exclusive to the M5 Pro model, also announced today. As Apple also notes, Thunderbolt 5 allows multiple M5 Pro Mac minis to run local AI models as a single cluster (for example, using something like exo ).

Alas, that won’t be possible with the M6 Mac mini and its Thunderbolt 4 bandwidth bottleneck. Nonetheless, I’d be intrigued to compare the performance of the widely regarded Qwen3. 8-27B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash models on the new M6 Mac mini.

Moving on to the flagship M5 Ultra Mac Studio, let’s start here:

With M5 Ultra, Mac Studio achieves up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra and a staggering 9.8x more than M1 Ultra. Combined with up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, 50 percent higher than before, Mac Studio lets users run massive models entirely on device with complete privacy — without counting tokens or worrying about rising cloud costs.

As seen on the Mac Studio’s product page, the 512 GB RAM version of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio will only be available in “late October”. Unlike the M6, the M5 Ultra supports Thunderbolt 5, which will allow customers to run multiple Mac Studios in a cluster with shared memory to distribute inference across machines. And, according to Apple, a cluster of four Mac Studios yields three times the performance of a single Mac Studio.

Speaking from personal experience, I know that my M3 Ultra Mac Studio using oMLX can run DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally with generation averaging 35 tokens/second. Assuming a linear 4x increase, that would put the same model at over 120 tokens/second on an M5 Ultra Mac Studio.

To put things in perspective, that kind of performance would be faster than any AI chatbot website, it’d be faster than many providers who offer a “fast” mode for their models, and it’d only be second to either dedicated NVIDIA PC clusters at home or specialized inference providers such as Cerebras or Groq …which are running in full-blown data centers.

Sure, you would need a computer that is likely going to cost more than $20,000 to make it happen, but it’d still be possible on a single machine that is small, quiet, and that – in theory – any consumer can buy off the shelf.

It’s also interesting to consider the implications of M5 Ultra for running much larger models that would have typically required aggressive quantization to even stay in memory and produce any useful output. For example, Z. ai’s GLM-5.

2 (a 744B MoE model) could run at up to 17 tokens/second on an M3 Ultra Mac Studio with 512 GB of RAM; the same person was even able to get the massive Kimi K3 model to run on a single machine…with decoding performance up to 3 tokens/second.

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: This Gamescom Showcase Did A Lot Of Games Dirty
articles.subtitle: It’s hard to criticize Gamescom’s Opening Night Live showcase without accidentally firing off shots at games that probably don’t deserve it, but that was a pretty miserable showcase.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
It’s hard to criticize Gamescom’s Opening Night Live showcase without accidentally firing off shots at games that probably don’t deserve it, but that was a pretty miserable showcase. Geoff Keighley hosts the biggest English-language video game showcases of the year, and the Germany-based presentation is typically the one that feels the least curated. This year, it also feels like the format is serving very few games on the stage.

If you were to pluck most of the trailers in the two-hour show out of the event, you probably could find a lot to be excited about. But the lineup at Gamescom hurt a lot of these games, as so many of them had such similar vibes, gameplay loops, and aesthetics that they all kind of blended together and painted a pretty stultifying picture of the months ahead.

I just wrote our recap for the showcase, and found that about midway through I was running out of things to say about every dark fantasy game, edgy shooter, or anime-inspired Hoyoverse-esque game as it came and went without a moment of impact.

Obviously, Keighley had a few major games up his sleeve to act as the headliners, but Final Fantasy VII Revelation ’s appearance was all too brief after we’d endured nearly two hours of games that couldn’t hope to meaningfully differentiate themselves from all the others.

The night’s final reveal, a remaster of The Witcher 3, was probably the biggest surprise of the show, which is kind of anticlimactic note to end on, as it’s an 11-year-old game. At least it’s getting a hefty expansion next year so there’s something new on the horizon.

This is the same struggle that shows like Wholesome Games have run into, in that they’re so curated around a specific theme that showing too many games at once runs the risk of them all bleeding into each other, and the longer the show goes on, the less time anyone gets to process something that looks cool before their short-term memory is overwritten by the next not-distinct-enough game.

This year’s Gamescom felt like the also-ran of Keighley’s shows.

Summer Game Fest has taken up E3’s usual place as the summer show that everyone pays attention to, and the Game Awards has prestige to chase as it positions itself as the video-game Oscars, which leaves Gamescom in this awkward spot of sometimes feeling like a place for Keighley and crew to dump all the miscellaneous games that aren’t quite big enough to headline one of the glitzier showcases.

And while some of these games will surely benefit from being featured here, it doesn’t do them any real favors to get overshadowed by Final Fantasy VII.

articles.subtitle: Macworld If you’re planning on investing in a new M6 Mac mini or M5 Ultra Mac Studio, you might be buying a new Apple Magic Keyboard along with it. Apple has updated its keyboards, too: Certain keys have had their labels changed to symbols instead of names.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
If you’re planning on investing in a new M6 Mac mini or M5 Ultra Mac Studio, you might be buying a new Apple Magic Keyboard along with it. Apple has updated its keyboards, too: Certain keys have had their labels changed to symbols instead of names.

Apple introduced these changes with the MacBook Neo and M5 MacBook Air, so the company is basically catching up on normalizing the keys. The Tab, Caps Lock, Shift, Delete, and Return keys no longer have their respective word labels. Instead, they have arrow icons:

Tab is now ⇥

Caps Lock is now ⇪

Shift is now ⇧

Delete is now ⌫

Return looks similar to ↵ (see photo above)

The switch to the graphical labeling is an effort to standardize its keyboards. Apple’s non-English keyboards have used symbols, and implementing them in the English keyboard streamlines the production process. However, Apple did not update the keys on the $129 wireless Magic Keyboard with Numeric Keypad that has a Lightning connection for charging.

Speaking of the production process, it appears that the Magic Keyboards have not been affected by the worldwide RAM shortage (/sarcasm), so their prices have not changed:

articles.title: Apple Announces New M6 and M5 Pro Mac minis, Along with M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studios
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.

The headline feature of the M6 chip is that it’s Apple’s first 2-nanometer chip. The chip also includes “a larger 12-core CPU complex with the world’s fastest CPU core, a larger 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and up to 170GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.”

Looking more closely at the M6, Apple says it consists of two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores and is 1.2x faster in multithreaded performance than an M5 and up to 2.4x faster than an M1. Apple says the GPU delivers nearly 30% more peak GPU compute for AI than the M5. The M6’s 10% faster memory bandwidth will help with AI tasks, too, but its 32GB memory ceiling will limit which models can run locally.

The M6 mini’s GPU sounds impressive, too, with two more cores, Neural Accelerators for each core, which is a first for the mini. According to Apple, that leads to an up to four-fold increase in AI performance and a 2x graphics bump compared to the M4 mini. The Neural Engine has also been improved.

Apple also introduced an M5 Pro mini. It’s understandable if you find it confusing that the base model Mac mini has a more recent generation chipset than the more expensive model. What matters more than the chip generation is the “Pro” in M5 Pro, which makes it more capable than the M6, which has been designed for entry-level models.

The same sort of asymmetry occurred with the 2025 Mac Studio, which included an M4 Max model alongside the M3 Ultra. A big part of that difference is the M5 Pro mini’s support for 64GB of memory (double the M6 version’s top memory spec) and its 307GB/s of memory bandwidth compared to the M6 model’s 170GB/s memory bandwidth.

As for the M5 Ultra, which debuts in the Mac Studio, it sounds like a beast. According to Apple, the chip uses a next-generation version of its UltraFusion technology, resulting in a quad-die architecture for the first time in an Apple silicon chip. In addition, the M5 Ultra features an “up-to-36-core CPU and up-to-80-core GPU with a massive 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, 50 percent more than M3 Ultra.”

Here’s what Sri Santhanam, Apple’s vice president of Silicon Engineering Group, had to say about the new chips:

Today, we’re debuting the next giant leap in performance and AI compute for Apple silicon with the incredibly advanced M6 and the most powerful M-series chip yet, M5 Ultra. Built using the cutting-edge 2 nm process, M6 combines a new CPU complex, two additional CPU and GPU cores, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and more unified memory bandwidth to power through workloads with amazing energy efficiency.

And for the ultimate desktop performance and the ability to run massive AI models, M5 Ultra features a massive GPU, now with Neural Accelerators, and more unified memory bandwidth, pushing the boundaries of what a desktop can do.

Apple is fusing two dual-die M5 Max chips to create a single quad-die architecture. Apple says the M5 Ultra is “up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than M3 Ultra”, the fastest Mac previously for sale. The M5 Ultra also supports up to an 80-core GPU with up to 4.5x the peak GPU compute for AI tasks compared to the M3 Ultra and features an upgraded Media Engine, according to Apple.

For those who don’t need the bleeding-edge performance of the M5 Ultra, Apple also introduced what sounds like a very capable M5 Max Mac Studio. The M5 Max version of the computer “features an 18-core CPU, an up-to-40-core GPU with Neural Accelerators built into each core, and up to 128GB of unified memory, accelerating complex pro and AI workloads.”

Macs featuring the new chips won’t be available immediately. You can preorder both online today for delivery on September 22 with the caveat that the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 512GB of memory won’t be available until later in October.

Prices have risen too. The Mac mini models are both $100 more than the models they replace, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio’s base configuration has risen $200. However, the M5 Max Mac Studio’s starting price hasn’t changed.

The Mac mini has been a lot of things to a lot of people over the years. From a compact, minimalist desktop system to a headless server, the mini is Apple’s jack-of-all-trades. More recently, demand for the tiny computer has surged as people put them to work for a variety of AI tasks, including running LLMs locally and serving as standalone Hermes and OpenClaw machines.

With memory and storage constraints, it’s no surprise that the base prices of the mini have risen. Despite those challenges, I hope Apple is able to produce enough to meet demand. I’ve loved having an M4 Pro model working away day and night in the background. It’s fast, relatively cool, energy efficient, and easy to run remotely.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Taking into account the existing 16 pieces of free Witcher 3 DLC and the more recent next-gen updates, those prices were already a good deal. You can't beat free, though.

articles.title: Tarae: The Unbound is an 'Eastern dark fantasy' action RPG, and I for one am here for K-Diablo
articles.subtitle: Featuring one of my favorite ARPG class archetypes: Guy With Gun.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
It brings me no joy to admit this, but recently I've begun thinking that I'm finally nearing my fill of ARPGs. I've gotten a lot of great years out of clicking a mouse button and exploding full screens of skeletons, but the prospect doesn't quite spark joy like it used to.

Or at least that's what I thought until roughly 45 minutes ago, when I saw the announcement trailer for Tarae: The Unbound that had been slipped into a Gamescom 2026 Opening Night Live Montage.

The problem, I now realize, is that I've mostly spent my time with ARPGs looking at the same kinds of things. Most games downstream of Diablo tend to flow into the same basin of interchangeable demons, dark cultists, and piles of weird meat. But looking at the brief clips of Tarae, I realize now I'd just been aching for a jolt to the ARPG aesthetic palette.

Developed by Boundary and published by Krafton, Tarae's Steam page says it's set in "a world that reimagines Eastern myth, folklore, and traditional aesthetics, where beauty and mystery are entwined with darkness and brutality." It shows in the listings screenshots and embedded gifs, where enemies are being fought in Buddhist temples and player characters are battling bosses with hauntingly distended features plucked from East Asian monster illustrations.

If that's not enough, Tarae: The Unbound also includes one of my favorite character class conceits: Just an old guy with a matchlock gun. Although this particular handgunner seems to know something I don't about how historic firearms work, because he's able to pump out rapid fire gouts of firebomb explosives. Good for him.

From the sounds of it, Boundary is aiming to offer a variety of buildcrafting systems: "The balance and conflict of the Five Elements, the harmony of Yin and Yang, karma and the cycle of reincarnation all shape your leveling, equipment, and combat style," the developer says. "Even within a single class, different choices lead to entirely different builds."

I can't begin to guess how that will all work in practice, but I'm eager to experience our K-Diablo future when the time comes. It likely won't be for a bit, however: Tarae: The Unbound doesn't have a release date, unlike the full release of Path of Exile 2 now pegged for December 11, but you can wishlist it on Steam now.

On a day of high-priced product announcements, Apple has offered a crumb of comfort to its more cash-strapped customers: the beloved Polishing Cloth has dropped in price by a whopping 53 percent. Relentlessly memed on for charging a faintly absurd $19 for the square cloth at launch three years ago, the company is now happy to accept just $9 for seemingly the same product.

The common thread uniting Tuesday’s two big Mac updates was prices going up. The M6 Mac mini starts at $899, up from $599 for the equivalent M4 model just two months ago. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio, meanwhile, starts at $5,499, a price hike of another $200 over the previous price hike. But the Polishing Cloth went against the grain with a huge price drop.

Apple didn’t send out a press release advertising the nonabrasive fabric accessory’s new bargain price. Instead, it quietly removed the previous store entry (which carried the product code MW693AM/A ) and put up a new one in its place ( MLH74AM/A ) with an updated price. Other than the price and code, it appears to be an identical product with an identical description.

As before, that includes the endlessly amusing Compatibility section, which lists every iPhone and iPad going back to 2012, every single Apple Watch, and a huge list of MacBooks. In some ways, it’s surprising the company bothered to make the list since the description makes it clear that the Polishing Cloth cleans any Apple display, but we appreciate the effort.

Whether this bargain price will last remains to be seen. Unlike other Apple devices the Polishing Cloth is unlikely to be affected by the ongoing memory shortage, but we’ll be monitoring international microfiber shipments with the greatest of interest.

articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Well, this seems interesting. ChatGPT’s latest update adds a new Mac integration: the ability to work with conversations from Apple’s Messages app. The feature works with iMessage, SMS, and RCS.

ChatGPT for Mac now includes an Apple Messages plugin

The new Apple Messages plugin lets ChatGPT read and search chats on a Mac, and prepare and send messages.

OpenAI says it is available across all plans in the ChatGPT desktop app for macOS, with support in both ChatGPT Work and Codex.

That access raises privacy and control questions, so OpenAI stresses that sending remains gated by user approval under the default settings.

Users should take care before granting persistent approval. OpenAI’s plugin guide details the risks and how to revoke access.

It also lists a known issue involving tasks that disable approval prompts: “If your task is set to Full access or otherwise disables approval prompts, Apple Messages may be unable to show the confirmation needed to send. Switch to Ask for approval or Approve for me and try again.”

How OpenAI’s Messages plugin works on the Mac

OpenAI explains that the optional Messages plugin runs locally on the Mac. Like other ChatGPT/Codex features including Computer Use, it relies on macOS system technologies like AppleScript and Accessibility.

The optional Messages plugin is not like the sketchy server-related hacks that try to bring iMessage functionality to Android. It’s simply using files on your Mac with your permission when prompted.

And unlike Siri AI, it doesn’t rely on an index of content from Messages. ChatGPT for Mac only uses the data when directed and with permission.

As you can see below, once enabled by the user, ChatGPT is super clear in what it does with messages, especially sending on your behalf when asked.

For these reasons, it shouldn’t be a privacy concern for Apple. The data exists as files on your Mac, and you need to give ChatGPT permission to work with the files. OpenAI also isn’t the only AI company to develop similar tools. It’s just a benefit of the Mac being a more capable operating system than mobile platforms.

Three AI features for video footage

articles.title: Apple announces the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with up to 512GB of RAM
articles.subtitle: Macworld While all eyes are on the upcoming iPhone event, Apple threw us a curveball Tuesday morning with a rare August launch of an updated Mac Studio with the all-new M5 Ultra processor.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
While all eyes are on the upcoming iPhone event, Apple threw us a curveball Tuesday morning with a rare August launch of an updated Mac Studio with the all-new M5 Ultra processor.

The new Mac Studio is visually identical to the previous model but has major upgrades inside. Instead of the M4 Max and M3 Ultra, you can now buy a Mac Studio with an M5 Max or M5 Ultra processor, with up to a whopping 512GB of RAM. Here are the specs Apple is offering for the two chips:

While the M5 Ultra is still double the capability of the M5 Max, Apple touts its “next-generation UltraFusion technology to form a quad-die architecture for the first time in an M-series chip.” The previous UltraFusion interconnector linked two Max dies over 10,000 high-speed connections that offer low latency and high bandwidth. It was previously reported that Apple was working to create a new version of the Ultra chip with more advanced UltraFusion architecture.

Apple is leaning hard into AI and calls the M5 Ultra Mac Studio “a game changer for AI workloads” and says “AI coding agents process significantly faster, image generation tools can render creations in an instant, and enterprise teams can cluster multiple systems to scale performance to new heights.”

In addition to the new chips, the Mac Studio now has an N1 chip to bring Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, as well as “a next-generation SSD architecture built on PCIe Gen 6.” We already praised the MacBook Pro for its super-fast storage speeds, and Apple now claims the new SSDs deliver “industry-leading read and write speeds for rapid project loading, file transfers, and loading huge LLMs.”

Now for the not-so-good news. While the M5 Max model starts at the same $2,499 as the post-price-hike M4 Max, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio now starts at $5,499, an increase of another $200 over the previous price hike. That means you’re paying $1,500 more than if you bought an M3 Ultra Mac Studio before June.

You’re also paying more for storage and RAM, so get ready to shell out well over 20 grand for a fully loaded model (which won’t be available until October). The most expensive M5 Ultra you can get now, with 256GB of RAM and 16TB of storage, costs $18,299.

The M5 Mac Studio is available for pre-order now but won’t begin shipping until September 22.

articles.title: Meta AI is now available as a more capable desktop app for Mac
articles.subtitle: Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI. Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI.

Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac

The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.

Based on initial inspection, it runs natively on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 15 or later, using an AppKit and SwiftUI shell with WebKit for richer chat content. In other words, this is not an Electron app or a repackaged iPad release.

It includes Mac-specific hooks, making the desktop experience more robust than the Meta AI mobile app.

Quick Invoke uses Option-Space to place a compact Meta AI composer over whatever you are doing. A separate dictation feature lets you hold a shortcut, speak, and have the resulting words typed into any app, from Mail and documents to code editors.

Meta AI can also attach another Mac window to a conversation. With Screen Recording and Accessibility permission, the app reads the window’s visible text and captures a screenshot for the next question. This is context gathering rather than computer control for now.

Beyond chat, the sidebar includes Media, Artifacts, scheduled tasks, conversation history, and an “About Me” personalization section.

Users can switch among thinking modes, attach files, generate media, and create recurring briefings or reminders. The app also includes the ability to hide the Dock icon, allowing it to be invoked with a keyboard shortcut instead.

Meta’s recent AI push

The Mac app is the latest in a steady run of releases. In April, Meta replaced Llama with Muse Spark. A May update then expanded Meta AI with more natural voice conversations and live camera-based assistance.

July brought Muse-powered image generation to Meta AI, WhatsApp, and Instagram, although Meta quickly removed one feature that generated images from public Instagram posts. Meta AI also moved into Threads DMs for private chats.

Most recently, Meta launched Muse Code, a terminal-based AI coding agent for macOS and Linux.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
If you still haven't played The Witcher 3, it might finally be time

While The Witcher 3 is often heralded as one of the best games of the century, if not all time, there's one problem with the legendary 2015 RPG: The part where you have to actually play it. CD Projekt Red seems intent on addressing some of those gameplay shortcomings and adding a new layer of visual polish with the newly announced The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered. And the best part? It's a free upgrade for those who already own the game.

The trailer for the remaster shows off noticeable graphical improvements that make the game look much more colorful, along with a new photo mode. Beyond the upgraded visuals, the remaster has a long list of gameplay updates. It will feature reworked combat, which was probably the weakest element of the original release.

Enemies have been reworked with "enhanced monster behaviors," and there are new finisher animations. Traversal also seems improved across the board: we see Geralt haul himself over fences and quickly scale ladders. The finicky horse riding has been updated as well, and we see the Witcher lean to the left and right in his saddle to avoid trees.

Beyond this, the skill tree has been revamped, and item management has been reworked. We see Geralt showing off some slick armor with the new transmogrification feature — for those unfamiliar with this term, it means you can choose one set of armor for Geralt's visual appearance and another that will impact his stats.

Lastly, those who own the base version of The Witcher 3 will be able to play its acclaimed expansions, Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine, for free. CD Projekt Red clearly wants to get as many players on The Witcher bandwagon as possible ahead of the studio's big upcoming releases.

In 2027, the studio will release The Witcher 3 — Songs of the Past, a major new expansion for the game. After that, the studio plans to release The Witcher 4 in 2028. Between The Witcher 3 remaster, which is out on Sept. 29, and everything else, there will be many excuses to play Gwent in the coming days. Thank goodness for that.

articles.author: MacRumors

Price Increases - The Mac mini now starts at $899, $300 over the original starting price of the M4 Mac mini when it launched in October 2024. Mac Studio pricing starts at $2,499, $500 more than the original price of the M4 Max model when it came out in March 2025.

Connectivity - Apple upgraded the new Macs with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, so they are on par with the connectivity standards in the latest iPhone models. Wi-Fi 7 offers faster data speeds in the 6GHz band, lower latency, and an option to connect across 2.4GHz, 5GHz, and 6GHz networks at once for reliability improvements.

Genlock - The ‌Mac mini‌ and ‌Mac Studio‌ support genlock over USB-C, so there's no need for a separate sync box. Genlock is used in multi-camera shoots and virtual production to lock timing to a shared reference signal. The Mac's display and the camera filming it are synchronized, preventing flickering and tearing from a mismatch between the display refresh rate and camera shutter.

Apple previously added genlock support to the iPhone 17 Pro models, so now an ‌iPhone 17 Pro‌ and one of the new Macs can work in tandem for pros who need the feature.

Ethernet - The ‌Mac mini‌ now starts with 2.5Gb Ethernet instead of 1Gb. There's an option to upgrade to 10Gb, which is what the ‌Mac Studio‌ starts with (same as the prior-generation model).

Neural Engine - The M6 chip has an upgraded Neural Engine with two 16-core engines instead of just one. Apple says the new Neural Engine offers 2x more peak compute so AI workflows run faster.

GPU - The M6 ‌Mac mini‌'s 12-core GPU has Neural Accelerators in each core, offering up to 4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than the ‌M4 Mac mini‌. The ‌Mac Studio‌'s M5 Ultra is also the first Ultra chip with Neural Accelerators. Peak AI compute performance is 4.3x the M3 Ultra's performance.

SSD - ‌Mac Studio‌ storage is twice as fast with new SSD architecture built on PCIe Gen 6.

SSD Pricing - As Daring Fireball points out, upgrading a ‌Mac mini‌ with a 2TB SSD costs $1,000, which is more than the $899 base price of the machine. Upgrading to the 4TB SSD for the M5 Pro costs $1,800, which is $100 over the price of the base machine.

Thunderbolt - The M6 ‌Mac mini‌ continues to have Thunderbolt 4, not Thunderbolt 5. The M5 Pro model does have Thunderbolt 5.

Current Max Pricing - An M5 Pro ‌Mac mini‌ with 18-core CPU, 64GB RAM, an 8TB SSD, and 10GbE is $6,799. The M5 Ultra ‌Mac Studio‌ with 36-core CPU, 256GB RAM, and 16TB SSD is $18,299.

512GB RAM - The M5 Ultra ‌Mac Studio‌ supports up to 512GB RAM, with the option coming in late October. Upgrading to 256GB RAM costs $4,000, and the 512GB option will be even more expensive. 96GB and 256GB RAM are the only options right now.

Announcement Timing - This is the first time Apple has announced new Macs in August since the 27-inch iMac debuted in August 2020.

articles.title: Apple launches new M6 Mac mini with another price hike
articles.subtitle: Macworld As predicted on this site earlier today, Apple has announced the launch of a new Mac mini model with M5 and M6 chip options.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
As predicted on this site earlier today, Apple has announced the launch of a new Mac mini model with M5 and M6 chip options. It doesn’t feature any design changes or external upgrades, but it does offer a two-generation bump in processors compared to the previous model.

Slightly confusingly, the version of the Mac mini with a chip from the M5 generation is the more powerful of the two, because it’s the M5 Pro. This spec starts at $1,699 for a 15-core CPU and 16-core GPU, but customers have the option to bump that to 18 and 20 cores, respectively, for an additional $200.

There are also configuration options to increase RAM from the starting 24GB or storage from the baseline 512GB, and to upgrade to 10 Gigabit Ethernet. The RAM options remain the same, but the 64GB highest-end option now costs $1,000.

More appealing for the Mac mini’s traditional budget market will be the M6 model, which starts at a far more manageable $899. That, however, is still a $100 increase over the M4 model from 2024 that it replaces. Worse, the M4 model started at just $599 until June, when Apple responded to the ongoing memory crunch by imposing brutal price hikes. In other words, the cheapest entry point to Apple’s desktop Mac ecosystem has jumped by $300, or 50 percent, in the space of two months.

The $899 version isn’t exactly a state-of-the-art build, either. The entry-level configuration comes with 16GB of RAM and just 256GB of storage. We should note that it is possible to get this spec for $799, but only if you’re an education buyer. Of note, the Mac mini is not available for the Apple Upgrade program either.

Apple

The price hike is likely to weaken the Mac mini’s appeal among budget buyers, but (aside from the necessity to accommodate increasing component costs) Apple may not care. In his report predicting that a new mini was on the way, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman noted that the machine had become increasingly popular for running AI applications locally, and that Apple was struggling to meet demand.

The company may not mind if fewer customers are prepared to pay the asking price, since there are plenty of AI fans ready to take their place.

Those AI fans will likely be tempted by a new model with a new chip. Apple boasts that the M6 delivers “gains across every dimension of performance” and “the ideal balance of performance, power efficiency, and on-device AI to effortlessly fly through daily tasks, coding, and creative projects.”

In numerical terms, the company claims the M6 version of the Mac will deliver up to 4x faster AI performance, 2x faster storage and graphics, and 40% faster CPU performance than the M4 mini. The M5 Pro model, meanwhile, is rated by its maker as up to 8.5x faster at LLM prompt processing than its M2 Pro predecessor, and up to 4x faster than the M4 Pro model. Naturally we will put those claims to the test in our labs.

Another surprise is how early Apple has announced the new Mac mini. Pre-orders are open now, but it won’t go on sale until 22 September, almost a month from now.

articles.title: Jungle Shot 11 Music Videos in Four Days with Apple Creator Studio
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.

The band’s toolbox included Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Pixelmator Pro to capture the series of signature one-shot take videos. According to the App Store feature on the band’s process, Logic Pro was where the entire album was produced. The app’s Varispeed feature was also used to shift the tempo of songs while maintaining pitch as they shot the videos.

Final Cut Pro’s Magnetic Mask was used to composite footage quickly. Jungle’s Tom McFarland told Apple:

Final Cut Pro is like a magic sword. There’s one shot for the track ‘Romeo II,’ where the camera accidentally caught some of the lighting rig. With five clicks, the editor was able to paint it out. It just automatically knows.

Pixelmator Pro on the iPad with an Apple Pencil and Mac enabled the band’s team to add artwork and posters to the final product, too.

But of all the quotes from the band, J Lloyd’s comment really struck a chord with me:

We didn’t have to worry about the tech. We could just focus on getting the design right. I could pick up the iPad between takes and keep sketching on Pixelmator Pro, and it all just worked.

I love apps, or I wouldn’t write about them every day, but what I love even more is the creativity they enable. Getting a glimpse of how one of my favorite bands uses some of the same tools I do was a treat.

articles.title: Paradox's next grand strategy game is taking cues from Fallout and Mad Max
articles.subtitle: Afterworld will let you conquer post-apocalyptic North America.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Paradox Development Studio is taking a break from conquering history and space, setting its sights instead on post-apocalyptic North America. Afterworld will see you take control of a tribe of survivors as you explore and conquer the ruins of the fallen continent. Which you might already know, after yesterday's leak. But now it's official!

Afterworld was just revealed during Gamescom's Opening Night Live, with a trailer that's evocative of both Fallout and Mad Max. Paradox has naturally put its own spin on things, however, with features like the Ancients, immortal leaders who existed before the collapse of civilisation, and who are now fighting to rule what's left using forgotten technology. They might cause some problems for you.

Like Stellaris, you'll be able to pick your tribe's origins, including a Fallout-inspired start that sees you leaving the safety of your bunker to begin a new life in the wasteland. There's a survival bent to the proceedings, with your tribe needing to scrounge up the bare necessities like food and water before it can start thriving. Unlike previous PDX games, you really are starting from scratch.

Eventually you'll be able to rebuild civilisation or create something completely new, founding new religions, establishing laws, and taking advantage of pre-Fall technology, like that big ol' spider robot from the trailer. With convoys you'll be able to set up trading routes and supply lines to keep your new civilisation ticking, and if things get too rough you can leave your home behind and migrate to a new land, or just become nomads or raiders.

Afterworld seems to be shaping up to be Paradox's most exploration-heavy grand strategy game—even when compared to Stellaris. Take the ideas tree, for instance. This is essentially your tech tree, and it's based entirely on what your tribe experiences.

Instead of seeing the whole tree laid out in front of you, or getting a random selection of techs to choose from, the tree is revealed through exploration. If your tribe encounters a river, you'll learn about irrigation, unlocking the appropriate idea in the tree. If you meet another tribe and they've established a religion, then you'll discover the organised religion idea.

This is also where the procedural generation can shake things up. While the terrain and geography are immutable, you'll encounter different tribes, resources and dangers when you start a new run. So you'll always be able to find that river and unlock irrigation, but other experiences will be random.

Afterworld's development is being led by Dan Lind, formerly game director on Hearts of Iron 4. But there seems to be plenty of concepts drawn from Paradox's other grand strategy games as well. I've mentioned Stellaris a couple of times already, but it looks like there's plenty of Crusader Kings DNA in here too. Even though you're running a tribe rather than inhabiting an individual ruler, it still seems like there are some RPG nods.

"Afterworld is Paradox’s first non-historical setting in a decade, and I can’t wait to see what stories our players will tell with it,” says Lind. "This is the first world we’ve gotten to build from scratch in a long time, and the first one we've had the pleasure of destroying before the game starts. The old world is still out there in fragments, waiting to be found. What comes after it is entirely up to the players."

I know a lot of PDX fans were hoping for a Stellaris-like fantasy game for the developer's next outing, but we've already got so many fantasy-themed 4X games—the post-apocalypse strikes me as a more novel GSG setting.

A couple of weeks ago I got to go hands-on with Afterworld, so keep an eye out for my preview soon.

articles.title: M6 and M5 Ultra Debut in Updated Mac mini and Mac Studio
articles.subtitle: We knew the M6 chip was coming, and it seemed likely Apple would produce an M5 Ultra chip, since it skipped the M4 generation for the Ultra.
articles.author: TidBITS
articles.content:
We knew the M6 chip was coming, and it seemed likely Apple would produce an M5 Ultra chip, since it skipped the M4 generation for the Ultra. But a late August release was unexpected and suggests Apple is clearing the decks before the early September announcements of new iPhone and Apple Watch models.

In a trio of announcements, Apple unveiled the M6 and M5 Ultra chips, revealed new Mac mini configurations with the M6 and M5 Pro, and raised the Mac performance ceiling with new Mac Studio models that use the M5 Max and M5 Ultra. The new Macs are available for pre-order now, with deliveries promised for 22 September 2026. We’ll see if Apple has predicted demand accurately enough to meet that promise for everyone who pre-orders.

I’ll admit that my eyes glazed over somewhat when I read these Apple chip and Mac announcements because there are so many picky details surrounding performance. If a friend who uses the Mac but doesn’t care about the details asked me about the changes, I’d say, “Everything is faster, but also more expensive.” For those who want the specifics, let’s dive in.

M6 and M5 Ultra

The M6 chip is the latest update in the evolution of Apple silicon. It’s the first chip to use a 2-nanometer process. Although that’s more of a marketing term than anything, chips using a 2-nanometer process can be faster and more power-efficient than those relying on a 3-nanometer process, as the M3 through M5 did.

Internally, the M6 features a “larger 12-core CPU complex with the world’s fastest CPU core, a larger 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and up to 170 GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.” That’s two more CPU and GPU cores than the M5, a single 16-core Neural Engine, and 10% more memory bandwidth.

The “CPU complex” is interesting. Previously, M-series CPUs differentiated between “performance” and “efficiency” cores, but with the M5, Apple renamed its highest performance cores from “performance” to “super. ” Then, in the M5 Pro and M5 Max, Apple introduced a new “performance” core that sits between “super” and “efficiency” cores.

The super cores focus on single-threaded performance, the performance cores handle multithreaded workloads, and the efficiency cores manage everyday background tasks.

The M6 has 2 super cores, 4 performance cores, and 6 efficiency cores, whereas the M5 had 4 super cores and 6 efficiency cores. Apple isn’t specifying how much faster the M6 is than the M5 in single-threaded super-core tasks, beyond saying it’s the “world’s fastest.” However, it’s 1.2x faster in multithreaded performance. Rather than repeat Apple’s benchmarks in running text, here’s a chart (thank you, Claude) that will give you a better sense of how the M6 compares to the M5 and the much older M1.

The M5 Ultra, Apple’s most powerful chip ever, comes with other architectural innovations. As with previous Ultra generations, the M5 Ultra combines two M5 Max chips, but since they’re dual-die chips, the result is Apple silicon’s first quad-die architecture. (The M3 Ultra connected two single-die M3 Max chips.

) There’s no practical benefit to users in a quad-die architecture, but it’s a huge win for Apple. The larger the die, the more difficult and expensive it is to manufacture because a defect can ruin the entire die. Dividing the design into smaller dies can substantially improve manufacturing yield and reduce costs.

The M5 Ultra’s specs are insane. It has an up-to-36-core CPU with 12 super cores and 24 performance cores, an up-to-80-core GPU, a 32-core Neural Engine, a more capable Media Engine, and support for up to 512 GB of memory with 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth. The M5 Ultra dispenses with efficiency cores entirely, devoting all CPU resources to super and performance cores. Here’s another performance comparison chart with numbers pulled from Apple’s announcement.

Mac mini with M6 and M5 Pro

Look at Apple hopping on the AI bandwagon with this press release headline: “Apple’s new Mac mini, featuring M6 and M5 Pro, delivers a massive leap in AI performance, supercharging the leading desktop for always-on agentic computing.” Or just use it as a normal Mac like the rest of us.

Remember what I said about “faster, but more expensive?” Here’s where that starts. The M6 model of the Mac mini compares extremely favorably to the previous M4 model, and those with older Mac mini models will see even more performance gains. Have another chart.

Want more performance yet? For that, you’ll need a Pro chip, but since the M6 just debuted, the next best option is the M5 Pro. Apple provides no comparisons between the M6 and M5 Pro, but based on previous generations, the M5 Pro should substantially outperform the M6 in multithreaded and GPU-intensive tasks, even though the M6 is newer. Here’s how it compares to the M4 Pro and M2 Pro models.

The only other changes are connectivity improvements: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and upgraded 2.5Gb Ethernet with a 10Gb option available. Those come thanks to Apple’s N1 wireless chip, which also adds Thread support. (Note that the M6 Mac mini supports Thunderbolt 4, whereas the M5 Pro version has Thunderbolt 5.)

That’s the faster. How about the more expensive? You’ll remember that Apple raised the price of the Mac mini several months ago (see “ Apple Raises Prices for Many Products,” 26 June 2026), with the base M4 model jumping from $599 to $799 and the M4 Pro model increasing from $1399 to $1599. Both new releases add $100 to the price, so the M6 Mac mini starts at $899 and the M5 Pro starts at $1699.

articles.title: Apple unveils M6, M5 Ultra chips and updates its desktop Macs
articles.subtitle: In a bit of a late-August surprise while the world awaits word on the next generation of iPhones, on Tuesday Apple announced two new processors, the M5 Ultra and M6, which help power new iterations of its Mac Studio and Mac mini desktop computers.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
In a bit of a late-August surprise while the world awaits word on the next generation of iPhones, on Tuesday Apple announced two new processors, the M5 Ultra and M6, which help power new iterations of its Mac Studio and Mac mini desktop computers. Both models are available to pre-order now and will ship on September 22 and will run macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Bridging the generations

The M6 chip kicks off Apple’s next chip generation, and is its first based on a 2-nanometer production process. It’s also got the first 12-core CPU in Apple’s base M-series chip line, up from 10 cores in the M4 and M5 generations.

Those CPU cores are in an interesting configuration: The M6 is the first Apple chip to mix all three of its CPU core types. The chip has six efficiency cores, four performance cores, and two super cores.

According to Apple, each core design is focused on a different primary task: efficiency cores are meant to sip power (useful when running simple background tasks); performance cores are optimized for complex, multi-threaded jobs; and super cores were created to offer the highest possible single-threaded performance.

Apple claims that this design results in record-setting single-threaded performance and up to 1.2x speed improvements over the M5 chip. The M6 also offers a dual 16-core Neural Engine, for on-device AI performance. Memory bandwidth peaks at 170GB/s, 10 percent faster than the M5.

Just as the new chip generation arrives, the previous one ( launched in October 2025 ) is completed. The M5 Ultra is Apple’s first new Ultra chip since it introduced the M3 Ultra in March 2025. Apple says it’s using the next generation of its UltraFusion technology to connect two dual-die M5 Max chips to make Apple silicon’s first quad-die chip. UltraFusion connects the two dies with bandwidth of more than 4.4TB/s, letting the four dies work as a single chip.

The M5 Ultra offers up to 36 CPU cores (12 super/24 performance), which Apple says results in up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than the M3 Ultra. It offers up to 80 GPU cores and up to 512GB of memory with 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth.

Meet the Mac mini

Previously available in M4 and M4 Pro configurations, the new Mac mini is available in M6 and M5 Pro chip options. The new base price is $899, up $100 from the previous base, for the same standard 16GB RAM/256GB storage configuration. The M5 Pro configuration starts at $1699, also up $100 from the model sold until Tuesday.

(But keep in mind, the M4 Mac mini was introduced at $599 before Apple recently raised that price. Put together, it’s a 50% price increase over the model introduced almost two years ago. We all know why, but it still hurts. )

Because the Mac mini previously shipped with M4 processors, this new model picks up numerous improvements Apple made in the M5 generation, including GPUs better optimized for AI performance. Both models support Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 via Apple’s N1 chip, and 2.5Gb Ethernet is now standard, with 10Gb Ethernet still available as an add-on. The M6 model supports Thunderbolt 4, but the M5 Pro model supports Thunderbolt 5.

Mac Studio advances in unison

At the same moment the Mac mini becomes split between two chip generations, the Mac Studio gets reunified with chips from the same generation: the M5 Max and the new M5 Ultra. As mentioned previously, the M5 Ultra is basically two M5 Max chips connected together by Apple’s dense, fast UltraFusion technology. Apple boasts that the M5 Ultra is the fastest chip Apple has ever created, which isn’t much of a stretch since the M5 Max was already pretty far up there.

The Mac Studio is effectively the replacement for the Mac Pro, and it’s alone in offering the Ultra-class chip. Apple has positioned the Mac Studio as ideal for local AI workflows, and the new models will still be able to cluster via Thunderbolt 5 to create even larger collections of memory and performance.

Apple representatives pointed out that a four-Mac Studio AI cluster, like the one I saw on display at WWDC earlier this summer, is so efficient that it can be powered from a single standard wall outlet. (They even showed us a picture of four Mac Studios plugged into a power strip that was plugged into the wall.

) In an era of data center excesses, Apple is clearly leaning into the possibility of small, efficient Macs being used to do local AI work rather than relying on huge, power-hungry cloud models.

As with the Mac mini, the Mac Studio gains M5 chip improvements that benefit AI models running on GPU cores, integrate the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, and support 2x faster storage with speeds up to 15GB/s.

articles.title: Hands-On with Computer History: OpenAI’s Take on Agent Memory
articles.subtitle: Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into...
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into Markdown memory files that serve as context for subsequent interactions.

The idea is that with the additional context, ChatGPT and Codex will better understand your requests, requiring you to provide less detail up front while getting better results. Anyone familiar with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and similar projects will know where this is going.

Here’s how it works.

Computer History is currently a Mac-only feature that is turned off by default, so if you want to try it, head to the Integrations section of the desktop app’s settings and toggle it on. History entries can be cleared individually, too. Before you get started, ChatGPT explains that you can pause or clear your history and manage the apps and websites that Computer History accesses at any time.

I excluded Passwords, 1Password, and Keychain Access to start and may add to that list as I use the feature more and get a better sense for the sort of information that it collects.

That opening alert also says you agree to pause Computer History during video and audio calls with others to avoid recording them without their consent. I appreciate the reminder that recording people without consent is something you shouldn’t do and is even illegal in some places, but as with the many meeting summarization tools on the market, I doubt that very many people will heed the warning and comply even though doing so is just a click of the menu bar away.

Still, I appreciate the alert up front, because turning Computer History on requires trust that the information won’t be misused by OpenAI. I’m sure that’s a bridge too far for some, but one of the most frustrating parts of using a tool like Codex is explaining yourself over and over. Every thread is like Groundhog Day for an agent, and while there are techniques that help provide continuity, making it automatic with Computer History is an exciting prospect.

If you’re intrigued by the potential, it pays to read OpenAI’s documentation and understand how the feature works. First of all, Computer History is not the same as Chronicle, a retired research preview feature that relied on taking screenshots as you worked.

In contrast, Computer History records interaction events but not screenshots, audio, or private web browsing sessions, according to OpenAI’s documentation. In practice, what that means is that as you work, ChatGPT will record your switches from app to app and what you’re doing in apps. Here’s what it’s captured as I started work on this story:

As you can see, every 10 minutes, ChatGPT creates a brief, timestamped summary of what I’ve been doing and lists the apps I’ve used by their icons. If I hover over an entry, I can immediately delete it or open the source file in the Finder for more detail on the information that ChatGPT is collecting.

Each entry in Computer History is a Markdown file with YAML front matter that includes a title, description, and list of the apps you’ve used followed by a structured memory document. Here, you’ll see a summary of what you’ve done:

The user continued writing computer history. md in Obsidian’s MacStories Vault, refining the section that explains how Computer History differs from the earlier Chronicle preview and adding a practical description of what the feature records while the user works.

The user referenced the OpenAI Learn Computer History documentation in Safari, briefly exchanged messages with Federico Viticci, checked ChatGPT/Codex settings, and then opened MacStories Images to queue a screenshot named CleanShot 2026-08-14 at 06. 08. 44@2x. png for upload. The upload was queued by the end of the segment, but no completed upload or copied Markdown image link was observed.

You’ll also find details that ChatGPT deems important and non-obvious, such as the following:

Important non-obvious context about the user MacStories Vault - Obsidian vault where the Computer History article draft was active. computer history. md - active note being drafted for the Computer History article. CleanShot 2026-08-14 at 06. 08. 44@2x. png - screenshot selected from @ Screenshots and queued in MacStories Images near the end of the window.

MacStories Images - internal Safari image uploader used for the screenshot; the page showed one queued item and an Upload 1 control. Federico Viticci - Messages conversation briefly active during the writing session. ChatGPT/Codex settings - ChatGPT app showed settings around 10:08Z, likely related to the same Computer History article context.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation. articles.title: The hardware crisis has hit a new low: We're now using rats for RAM
articles.subtitle: Rat computer.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Good news from the near future: Space travel has apparently advanced enough to allow humanity to establish a hotel on the surface of the moon.

Bad news: The RAMpocalypse apparently continues unabated, forcing novel experimentation with alternate forms of computer memory not rendered wholly unaffordable by AI datacenters. Namely, rat computers.

This believable projection of the current miserable state of consumer hardware comes courtesy of Ontos, the next game from Amnesia developer Frictional Games. In the trailer above, a man strapped to a chair with electrodes stuck in his head is a bit freaky, though less so than another guy who's missing everything from his upper teeth down; perhaps humanity in the future is so desperate for localized processing power that we're resorting to shoving DisplayPort cables into our brains, too.

The strongest big of imagery in the trailer by far, though, is a computer the size of a wall with 60 rats connected to it in sequence. Or parallel? I'm not great on my circuitry fundamentals, but I know a rat computer when I see one.

I am instinctively scared of the rat computer and the unknown potential of 60 rat minds taking the place of random access asiago memory.

My fear is apparently warranted, given the ominous question posed in the trailer's YouTube description is as follows:

"Do you follow the instructions given through the rodent machine?

Do you seek an alternative approach?

Or simply sabotage the experiment to satisfy your own morbid curiosity?"

The description claims there is "no right or wrong solution in Ontos," but I think the subtext is clear: We must do whatever possible to avoid this future coming to pass. Let's call off this whole AI thing before the next hardware generation arrives, lest Dire Digital Rattus 6 become the only memory accepted by motherboards by the year 2030.

Assuming we even have that much time. Ontos is out next year, and might be a banger; we loved Frictional's last game, Amnesia: The Bunker, scoring it a 93%.

articles.title: Surprise report: New Mac mini could land any day now
articles.subtitle: Macworld Apple may yet spring one final surprise of the Tim Cook era, with a new report raising hopes that the company plans to launch an updated version of the Mac mini “as soon as the coming days.” (Update: it’s now been announced.) Writing for...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Apple may yet spring one final surprise of the Tim Cook era, with a new report raising hopes that the company plans to launch an updated version of the Mac mini “as soon as the coming days.” (Update: it’s now been announced.)

Writing for Bloomberg, well-connected leaker Mark Gurman says Apple is gearing up to unveil the first new Mac mini in almost two years. He bases this on the testimony of unnamed sources “familiar with the matter.”

The last Mac mini model, announced on October 29, 2024, featured a major redesign (it was significantly smaller than its predecessor) as well as a faster M4 chip. This machine has become extremely popular, Gurman says, for running AI applications, but the ongoing memory crunch means Apple has struggled to meet demand. The Mac mini has essentially been out of stock since the spring, with delivery times slipping into months-long waits.

That isn’t to say that Apple necessarily thinks the new model will help in this regard. Gurman acknowledges that it’s unclear “how the new model will affect wait times,” as an updated mini is unlikely to require less memory than the current one. It seems more likely that Apple simply feels it’s time for an update, and the product’s popularity has pushed it to the front of the line.

Gurman’s report is generally short on details, with little information offered regarding design (although we can guess that another redesign would be a surprise so soon after the last one) and tech specs, where he says only that models with both M5 and M6 chips have been tested. The main takeaway regards timings.

Gurman says the new Mac mini could arrive ahead of the iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro, which will appear in early September and likely on September 9, and even says it will likely be the last product to launch under Cook’s watch.

Cook is slated to exit the CEO seat on September 1, which (assuming Gurman’s speculation is correct) gives a window of just seven days for the Mac mini to arrive. And we can rule out most of those days because they’re unsuitable for an announcement; by far the most plausible are Tuesday and Wednesday of this week. It could launch today, in other words.

The mini is only one of the Macs getting an update this fall as part of a massive overhaul. For all the latest news and rumors, bookmark our regularly updated new Mac mini superguide.
